items.title: Declarations of Pecuniary Interest under the “Municipal Conflict of Interest Act”
CSD-SEN-26-001, Sunnyside Home Medical Director’s Report 2025
notes:
Julie Wheeler, Director, Seniors' Services, provided a brief introduction to the report and introduced Dr. Fred Mather, Medical Director, Sunnyside Home, noting his recent accomplishment of receiving the King Charles Coronation Medal in recognition of his contributions to the long-term care sector.

Dr. Mather provided a presentation on the annual Medical Director's Report from Sunnyside long-term care home, highlighting Sunnyside's focus on providing high quality care and a welcoming community. A copy of the presentation is attached to the agenda.

Dr. Mather outlined the spectrum of housing supports that Sunnyside provides for seniors, including Alzheimer's disease programs and supports. He also highlighted several performance indicators from the Canadian Institute for Health Information's long-term care dashboard, noting that Sunnyside is at a similar level to the provincial average statistic for the use of restraints and is below the provincial average for instances of potentially inappropriate use of anti-psychotics.

Dr. Mather highlighted the Living Classroom Personal Support Worker Program, which is a partnership between the Region of Waterloo and St. Louis Adult Learning and Continuing Education, noting the success of the program and positive experiences of students. He also noted that Sunnyside has received funding through the Canadian Institute of Health Research and the Canadian Consortium on Neurodegeneration in Aging for a four-year research project on trauma-informed care in long-term care homes that will begin later this year.

He also briefly reviewed Sunnyside's policy on advanced care planning and consent for care, noting that the policy is due for review.

In response to the Committee, Dr. Mather clarified how physical restraints are defined, noting an individual's ability to release themselves from a device determines if the device is considered a restraint, also noting that there is some nuance involved in determining restraints. Some devices, such as personal assistance safety devices, which are typically in place for an individual's comfort, may be considered restraints under this definition.

Dr. Mather also clarified that appropriate use of anti-psychotic drugs typically falls into one of five categories, including treatment for schizophrenia, Huntington's dementia, hallucinations, delusions, and end-of-life care. He stated that potentially inappropriate use within a long-term care setting might include treatment of aggressive behaviours in Alzheimer patients, noting that anti-psychotics have a very limited role in effectively treating these behaviours. 

Dr. Mather further clarified that Sunnyside's focus is on utilizing safer non-pharmacological interventions to ensure patient safety, including bed alarms and low bed heights, rather than other options such as bed rails that may introduce additional risks to patient safety.

Dr. Mather confirmed that the Living Classroom Personal Support Worker Program trains students on a spectrum of mental health and neurological conditions, as well as on trauma-informed approaches to care. He also discussed that as part of the first phase of the four-year research project taking place at Sunnyside, effects of the trauma of the Covid-19 pandemic on long-term care residents will be examined, as well as other more general effects that past trauma can have on individuals living in long-term care homes. He clarified that all residents have a care plan that includes all members of the individual's care team, including personal support workers, that ensures the safety of both residents and staff.

J. Gowing joined the meeting at 10:56 a.m. 

In response to the Committee, J. Wheeler noted that Sunnyside has begun implementing artificial intelligence tools to combat resident isolation and loneliness and has begun working with other partners to explore this area further.

S. Foxton left the meeting at 11:17 a.m.

Dr. Mather clarified that the trauma-informed care research project is being carried out in collaboration with Hillel Lodge in Ottawa and St. Joseph's Health Centre in Guelph. J. Wheeler also noted that Sunnyside emphasizes knowledge sharing and resource sharing where appropriate amongst long-term care homes to foster continued improvement within the health care sector. She also emphasized the importance of learning from all areas of the health care sector, including from private long-term care homes.

Received for information.

items.title: Strategic Priority - Equitable Services and Opportunities
PHP-HPE-26-002, 2025 Food Safety Program Report
notes:
Dr. Hsiu-Li Wang, Medical Officer of Health, provided an overview of the 2025 Food Safety Program report, noting that the program ensures compliance with provincial food safety regulations and carries out routine inspections of food premises, investigation of complaints, review of special events, and facilitation of licensing requests.

In response to an increased volume of work as a result of Region of Waterloo's population growth in recent years, Public Health has implemented a risk-based approach to prioritize inspections and reduce potential health impacts on the community. Dr. Wang noted that two public health inspector positions were added in 2025 in order to maintain high levels of service in a growing food safety program.

S. Foxton joined the meeting at 11:32 a.m. 

In response to the Committee, Aldo Franco, Director, Health Protection and Healthy Environments, clarified that Public Health strives to establish relationships with business owners and offer support on an individualized basis for completing necessary forms and processes related to food safety. He confirmed that the website e-form for the establishment of new food premises has been streamlined from previous versions and that Public Health does take feedback from the community into account when updating forms and processes. He also noted that Public Health meets as requested with special event operators to help provide education and review special event requirements, also noting that Public Health sits on several area municipality working groups on special events to provide support.

A. Franco noted that Public Health saw an increase in special events that were assessed last year, and that since the completion of last year's food safety program report, a video tutorial has been created and posted to the Public Health webpage to educate the community on food safety practices for special events. He also noted that education sessions have been completed with food premise operators upon request.

In response to the Committee, A. Franco clarified that during special events, operators are encouraged to publicly display "Check It, We Inspect It" signage, but that this is not required. He also noted that inspections are becoming increasingly complex as food premise operators continue to innovate their practices with creative new ideas.

Received for information.

items.title: PHP-PSV-26-001, Paramedic Services' 2025 Response Time Performance Plan Results
notes:
John Riches, Chief, Paramedic Services, provided a combined presentation on Paramedic Services' 2025 Response Time Performance Plan Results and Paramedic Services' Annual Key Performance Measurement Indicators. A copy of the presentation is attached to the agenda.

D. Craig joined the meeting at 11:38 a.m.

J. Riches acknowledged the investments from Council and other support that has helped Paramedic Services to achieve their recent improvements to service delivery.

J. Riches highlighted that despite an increase in vehicle responses, there were improvements to response times and to ambulance offload delays, and a decrease in unit utilization, code zero events, missed staff meal break compliance, and end-of-shift overtime for staff.

J. Riches also reviewed mitigation strategies that are being deployed in partnership with hospitals to combat ambulance offload delays, including the Designated Offload Nurse Program, continued expansion of Patient Care Model Standards options, advancement of Community Paramedicine Program, implementation of superintendents in the Cambridge Central Ambulance Communication Centre, implementation of the Medical Priority Dispatch System, emergency response units being staffed with advanced care paramedics, a Clinical Response Strategy for all areas of the Region, and deployment adjustments made according to current data. 

In response to the Committee, J. Riches confirmed that Cambridge Memorial Hospital has the highest number of offload delay hours in comparison with the Region's other hospitals, but that the hospital is working on continued improvements. He also noted that all hospitals in the Region have shown great improvements to offload delay times, explaining that senior hospital leadership buy-in on improving offload delays and the Ministry of Health's prioritization of this issue has contributed significantly to improvements.

In response to the Committee, J. Riches confirmed that the Paramedic Services Master Plan is used to inform annual budget asks, but noted that not all strategies within the Master Plan require financial investment. He also noted that the provincially funded Community Paramedicine Program currently responds to approximately 10% of paramedic calls and that there is a traditional 911 response for the remaining 90% of calls, with the eventual goal being that the Community Paramedicine Program would respond to 25-30% of calls.

In response to the Committee, J. Riches noted that 911 is called in some instances for non-emergency situations because patients are unable to or unsure of how to access other healthcare providers. He also noted that several public information sessions were held prior to the implementation of the Medical Priority Dispatch System.

C. James left the meeting at 12:00 p.m.

J. Riches clarified that dynamic deployment is used so that ambulances and emergency response units can be redirected to where they are needed regardless of where they have been initially stationed.

M. Harris left the meeting at 12:11 p.m. 

Received for information.
